Hon'ble J.J. Munir,J.
Hon'ble Anil Kumar-X,J.
This writ petition has been filed seeking to quash the impugned FIR dated 10.05.2025 giving rise to Case Crime No. 268 of 2025, under Sections 419, 420, 467, 468, 471, 406, 504, 120-B IPC, P.S.
Katghar, District Moradabad.
A reading of the FIR shows a thoroughly worked out crime of cheating a citizen of his hard-earned money, but with much fault on the informant's part also.

It was represented to the informant by one Ashish Jain, who portrayed himself to be an official of the Nagar Nigam, Moradabad, that he would ensure a contract for supply of cameras for the Nigam and a Wi-Fi project that was under the charge of the Nagar Nigam, Mordabad, sponsored by the Government of India.
Ashish Jain invited the complainant to meet two other men, to wit, Anil son of Ramlal and Sundar @ Surendra Singh son of Khem Singh (the petitioner).

These three men further persuaded the complainant that the contract for the supply of cameras and managing the Wi-Fi would be ensured for him, but, for this purpose,
he would have to shell out a sum of Rs. 2 crores to be paid in bribe to higher officers.
For the present, he would have to part with a sum of Rs. 1 crore.

These three men went to a certain hotel,
where they made the informant meet with another man by the name, Mujibur-rahman, who added Sundar @ Surendra Singh vs State Of U.P. And 3 Others on 5 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/58488659/
1 to the assurance given by others.

sentences.text: Still two other persons, who were called in, were Rishipal and Prabha.
Prabha was represented to be some Clerk in the Nagar Nigam, Moradabad.
All of them took the informant's Aadhar Card, PAN Card and Bank papers and made him sign certain documents for the purpose of securing a contract for him.

The informant then transferred in the specified account indicated by the petitioner, a sum of Rs. 49,00,000/- from his account maintained with the HDFC Bank, and further a sum of Rs. 51,00,000/- from another account maintained with the same Bank.
The transferree's account was maintained with the Indian Bank.
The complainant went back to his home at Faridabad in Haryana.

When after a week, the informant contacted Ashish Jain and asked about award of the promised contract and did not get a satisfactory answer, he came over to Moradabad and contacted the Indian Bank, Branch Kohinoor Tiraha, Moradabad, where the transferee's account was maintained.
He was horrified to find that the account was on hold.
Upon further inquiries, it was revealed that the account belonged to an NGO, where there was some dispute, on account of which, the account was put on hold.
The Bank Manager advised the informant that his money would be returned, but he should not send a mail confirmation from his ID.
The information discloses that the swindlers involved, fabricated a mail ID of the informant's and drew a sum of Rs. 20-25 lacs, out of those credited.
It was then that the informant reported the matter to the Police on 29.03.2025.

After some proceedings of investigation, the Manager, after seeking consent from the members of the NGO, transferred a sum of Rs. 52,04,058/- to the informant's account, whereas the other was taken away, swindling the informant.
Learned Counsel for the petitioner, in the face of such formidably damning facts, has very valiantly argued that the petitioner runs an NGO to which the informant had donated a sum of Rs. one crore.
It is said that the NGO works for the upliftment of the poor.
Ex facie it defies all logic, why a man, who contributes to an NGO working for the upliftment of the poor, would suddenly donate a sum of Rs. one crore, however rich he might be.

On the other side is the fact that there is a definitive allegation of the informant being swindled into the deal for making this sum of Rs. one crore being transferred in order to secure a Government contract entrusted to the management of the Nagar Nigam, Moradabad.
We must remark that the faith of our citizens in dubious ways has reached dangerous levels.
Everyone seems to believe that no benefit of any kind can come by meritorious pursuit.
Everyone believes that it comes by underhand deals and red tape.

It is the result of this generally prevalent impression in society, where the average citizens have sunk into the cynicism of thinking that everything done is achieved by some deceit or unfair means that individuals are led into such traps.
The conduct of the informant is not above board and may itself constitute an offence.
Nevertheless, so far as the petitioner is concerned, he is, in our considered opinion, not entitled to the slightest of relief.
The writ petition is rejected.
